title: Like ...: Actions
tagline: how people and things move, work and behave
why: Verb + like + noun similes describe how something is done: how deeply you sleep, how fast news travels, how smoothly a plan works. They are everywhere in conversation, sports commentary and journalism.
know: the frame verb + like + noun and eight high-frequency action similes
which verbs each simile goes with (sell like hot cakes, spread like wildfire)
understand: why like, not as, introduces a noun after a verb
the difference in tone between praise (fit like a glove) and criticism (drink like a fish)
able: describe habits, success and speed with natural action similes
change tense and subject freely while keeping the fixed noun
judge register, from neutral (spread like wildfire) to slangy (like a bat out of hell)
mistakes: The rumour spread as wildfire through the office.
The rumour spread like wildfire. Before a noun after a verb, use like; as means in the role of.
Her new novel is selling like hot bread.
Selling like hot cakes (or hotcakes). A literal translation (e.g. French petits pains) sounds odd in English.
I slept like a stone after the hike.
I slept like a log. English also says slept like a baby, but not a stone.
The wedding went as a clockwork.
The wedding went like clockwork. No article: clockwork is uncountable.
He took to golf like a fish to water.
He took to golf like a duck to water. The animal is fixed.
bigidea: After a verb, English uses like + noun to compare how something happens: she sleeps like a log, it fits like a glove. Using as here changes the meaning: he worked as a horse would mean that was his job.
Action similes package a whole picture into one phrase. Spread like wildfire tells you the speed, the danger and the impossibility of stopping it. That's why journalists and commentators love them.
The verb and the noun usually come as a pair. Things sell like hot cakes, rumours spread like wildfire, plans go or run like clockwork. Change the tense or the subject, but keep the pair together.
hidden: My brother drives like a maniac on the 401.
The choir's soprano sings like an angel.
The news of the layoffs hit me like a train.
We worked like dogs all summer to finish the cottage.
As soon as the bell rang, the kids took off like a shot.
The new manager watches us like a hawk.
After the long shift I went out like a light.

expressions.meaning: sleep very deeply and without waking
expressions.example: After a day of skiing at Blue Mountain, we all slept like logs.
expressions.bend: Any tense: I slept like a log, you'll sleep like a log. Plural: slept like logs.
expressions.note: Near-synonyms: sleep like a baby (peacefully), go out like a light (fall asleep instantly). Not like a stone.

expressions.example: Our teenage son eats like a horse; we buy milk every two days.
expressions.bend: Usually present simple for habits. Opposite: eat like a bird (very little).
expressions.note: Fine for family and friends; saying it to or about a woman you don't know well may sound rude.

pic.label: wildfire (a fire spreading through a forest)

expressions.example: The video of the moose in the mall spread like wildfire online.
expressions.bend: Used with news, rumours, panic, trends and diseases. Any tense. Not spread like fire.
expressions.note: Neutral enough for news reports. In Canada and California the literal image is very real, so it carries extra force.

expressions.meaning: sell very quickly and in large numbers
expressions.example: Heat pumps are selling like hot cakes since the rebate was announced.
expressions.bend: Also spelled hotcakes. Usually progressive or past: they're selling / they sold like hot cakes.
expressions.note: Hot cakes are pancakes, which sold fast at fairs. Don't translate a local version like hot bread.

expressions.example: The suit I found at the thrift store fits like a glove.
expressions.bend: For clothes, but also jobs and roles: the new role fits her like a glove. Add an object: fits me like a glove.
expressions.note: Always positive. Compare suit someone down to the ground (British): be perfect for someone.

pic.label: a charm (a lucky object, like a four-leaf clover)

expressions.meaning: work perfectly, often better than expected
expressions.example: I tried turning it off and on again, and it worked like a charm.
expressions.bend: Usually past simple: it worked like a charm. Variant: work like a dream (British leaning).
expressions.note: A charm is a magic spell, so the idea is that it worked almost magically. About methods and tricks, not people working hard.

expressions.meaning: happen exactly as planned, with no problems
expressions.example: Thanks to the volunteers, the marathon went like clockwork.
expressions.bend: Go or run like clockwork. Related: as regular as clockwork (happening at the same time every time).
expressions.note: No article: not like a clockwork. Good in work emails and reports.

expressions.e: take to something like a duck to water
expressions.meaning: learn or adapt to something naturally and easily
expressions.example: My mother took to her tablet like a duck to water.
expressions.bend: Pattern: take to + noun/ing + like a duck to water. Usually past: she took to teaching like a duck to water.
expressions.note: The verb is take to (begin to like or do well). Not like a fish to water. Always positive and admiring.

culture.how: Josef K. is arrested one morning and spends the novel fighting a court that never tells him his crime. At the very end, as he is put to death, his final thought is that he is dying like a dog, and he feels the shame will outlive him. Two words of action simile sum up a whole life without dignity.
culture.ask: English has many like a dog similes: work like a dog, be treated like a dog, die like a dog. Why do you think dogs appear in so many negative action similes?
culture.find: Kafka The Trial ending Josef K. like a dog

culture.how: This six-line poem shows an eagle perched high on a cliff above the sea, watching. In the final line the bird drops, and Tennyson compares its sudden dive to a thunderbolt. One action simile carries all the speed and power of the poem.
culture.ask: What action in sport or nature would you describe with a thunderbolt simile? Why?

culture.how: The Canadian songwriter compares the overwhelming, uncontrollable feeling of being drawn to someone to being caught in a hurricane. The long guitar solos make the storm audible. Like spread like wildfire, it pictures a force you can't resist.
culture.ask: Which is the better image for falling in love: a hurricane, wildfire, or something calmer? Why?

culture.how: Seger looks back at himself as a strong, steady young man and compares him to a rock, then wonders where that strength went. The song later became famous in Chevrolet truck commercials, where the simile sold toughness and reliability.
culture.ask: Is it fair for advertisers to use a song about lost youth to sell trucks? What changes when a simile becomes a slogan?

match.why: A log lies still and doesn't wake up.
Horses eat large amounts. Opposite: eat like a bird.
News, rumours and trends spread like wildfire.
Hot cakes are pancakes, popular at fairs.
Clothes, jobs and roles can all fit like a glove.
A charm is a magic spell.
Like the precise parts of a clock. No article.

match.l: take to something like a duck to water

sort.h: Sort the similes: do they describe habits of the body, success and things going well, or speed and force?

items.why: Drinking a lot of alcohol, as a habit. Critical.
Smoking a lot. Critical or humorous.

items.w: drive like a bat out of hell
items.why: Go dangerously fast. Informal; hell may offend some listeners.

items.w: come down on someone like a ton of bricks
items.why: Punish or criticise someone very severely.

pick.q: The cabin was so quiet that I ___ for ten hours.
pick.why: Sleeping deeply = slept like a log.

pick.q: Since he started playing hockey twice a day, our nephew ___.
pick.why: Eating very large amounts = eats like a horse.

pick.q: Within an hour, the rumour about the mayor's resignation had ___.
pick.why: Spreading fast and uncontrollably = spread like wildfire.

pick.q: The bakery's maple butter tarts are ___ at the farmers' market.
pick.why: Selling fast = selling like hot cakes.

pick.q: My daughter's wedding dress needed no changes. It ___.
pick.why: A perfect fit = fit like a glove. North Americans often use fit as the past form.

pick.q: I put a slice of apple in the bag of hard brown sugar, and it ___.
pick.why: A trick that worked perfectly = worked like a charm.

pick.q: The move to the new office ___; nobody lost a single file.
opts: took to it like a duck to water
pick.why: Happened exactly as planned = went like clockwork.

pick.q: She'd never coached before, but she ___ and won the league.
opts: took to it like a duck to water
pick.why: Adapted naturally = took to it like a duck to water.

spot.q: After the night shift I slept like a rock until noon.
spot.why: The fixed simile is sleep like a log.

spot.q: Panic spread like fire through the stadium when the lights went out.
spot.why: The noun is wildfire: fast and out of control.

spot.q: The new phones sold like warm bread on launch day.
The concert evacuation went like a clockwork.
My father took to retirement like a fish to water.
spot.why: The fixed image is a duck taking to water.

type.q: The camping trip wore the kids out, and they slept like ___.
type.why: Sleep like a log: plural logs with a plural subject.

type.q: Don't worry about cooking too much. My brother eats like a ___.
type.why: Eat like a horse: eat a lot.

type.q: News of the plant closure spread like ___ through the town.
Her memoir is selling like hot ___ in Ottawa bookstores.
type.why: Sell like hot cakes: sell very quickly.

type.q: The new knee brace fits like a ___.
type.why: Fit like a glove: fit perfectly.

type.q: I tried vinegar on the stain and it worked like a ___.
type.why: Work like a charm (or a dream): work perfectly.

bend.q: A teenager is describing a fast getaway to a friend. Which version sounds natural in that casual register? ___
opts: He drove off like a bat out of hell.
He drove off as a bat out of hell.
He drove off like the bat of hell out.
bend.why: Like a bat out of hell is fine among friends but too strong for formal writing.

bend.q: A British colleague praises a tip you gave her. Which variation sounds natural? ___
opts: Your tip worked like a dream.
Your tip worked as a dream.
Your tip dreamed like a charm.
bend.why: Work like a dream is a common variant of work like a charm.

bend.q: Which version describes a reliable bus schedule naturally? ___
opts: The 7:15 bus arrives as regular as clockwork.
The 7:15 bus arrives as regular like a clockwork.
The 7:15 bus arrives clockwork as regular.
bend.why: As regular as clockwork is the as ... as cousin of go like clockwork.

bend.q: Which version sounds natural about a new hire who fits her team perfectly? ___
opts: The job fits her like a glove.
The job fits like her a glove.
The job is fitting as a glove to her.
bend.why: The object (her) goes right after fits, and the simile stays fixed.

talk: Kafka's hero feels he dies like a dog. Which animal would you use in a like a ... simile to describe how you work or study? Why?
Neil Young and Bob Seger use simple title similes. Invent a Like a ... song title about your own life and explain it.
Role-play: you're planning a family reunion. Describe what went like clockwork, what sold like hot cakes at the bake table, and who slept like a log afterwards.
Tell a story about something you took to like a duck to water, and something you didn't.
Bad news seems to spread like wildfire online. Should social media companies slow it down? Use at least three similes from this lesson.

match.why: Often an instruction or encouragement: run like the wind!

match.r: drink a lot of alcohol regularly
match.why: Critical. Fish seem to drink all the time.
Often siblings or couples. Mainly North American; Britons also say fight like cat and dog.

match.l: come down on someone like a ton of bricks
match.why: Heavy and sudden. Mainly British, also heard in Canada.
As fast as switching off a lamp.
Like a chimney giving off smoke all day.

pick.q: When the dog got off its leash, my son ___ after it.
pick.why: Running very fast = ran like the wind.

pick.q: Her uncle ___ for years before he finally joined AA.
pick.why: Drinking heavily = drank like a fish.

pick.q: My twin sisters ___ as kids, but now they're best friends.
pick.why: Arguing constantly = fought like cats and dogs.

pick.q: If the inspector finds any safety violations, head office will ___.
opts: come down on us like a ton of bricks
take to us like a duck to water
pick.why: Severe punishment = come down on us like a ton of bricks.

pick.q: The baby ___ as soon as we started the car.
pick.why: Fell asleep instantly = went out like a light.

pick.q: My grandfather ___ until the doctor showed him his X-rays.
pick.why: Smoking heavily = smoked like a chimney.

spot.q: When the alarm rang, the children ran like the air to the exit.
spot.why: The fixed simile is run like the wind.

spot.q: My neighbours fight like cats and mice every weekend.
spot.why: Cats and dogs argue; cat and mouse is a different idea (a chase).

spot.q: The boss came down on him like a ton of rocks for missing the deadline.
After the long flight I went out as a light.
spot.why: After a verb, use like + noun.

type.q: Grab the umbrella and run like the ___ before the bus leaves.
type.why: Run like the wind: run very fast.

type.q: At university he drank like a ___, but he's teetotal now.
type.why: Drink like a fish: drink heavily.

type.q: Those two have fought like cats and ___ since kindergarten.
type.why: Fight like cats and dogs: argue constantly.

type.q: If you're late again, the manager will come down on you like a ton of ___.
type.why: Like a ton of bricks: very severely.

type.q: I was so tired that I went out like a ___ on the sofa.
type.why: Go out like a light: fall asleep instantly.

type.q: My first landlord smoked like a ___ and the walls were yellow.
type.why: Smoke like a chimney: smoke heavily.

bank.q: Fresh air and a long paddle, and I ___ last night.
bank.why: Slept deeply = slept like a log.

bank.q: For someone so slim, my roommate ___.
bank.why: Eats a lot = eats like a horse.

bank.q: The fake story about the prime minister ___ on social media.
bank.why: Spread fast and out of control = spread like wildfire.

bank.q: The team's Stanley Cup shirts ___ after the final.
bank.why: Sold quickly = sold like hot cakes.

bank.q: The part of the stern headmistress suited the veteran actor; it ___.
bank.why: A role that suits someone perfectly fits them like a glove.

bank.q: I offered the toddler a sticker to get into the car seat, and it ___.
bank.why: A trick that worked perfectly = worked like a charm.

bank.q: Thanks to careful planning, the city's election night ___.
bank.why: Happened smoothly as planned = went like clockwork.

bank.q: My retired neighbour started painting last year and ___.
opts: took to it like a duck to water
bank.a: took to it like a duck to water
bank.why: Adapted naturally and quickly = took to it like a duck to water.

bank.q: The baby finally slept like a ___ after her bath.
bank.why: Sleep like a log (or ironically, like a baby): sleep deeply.

bank.q: Word of the free concert spread like ___ across campus.
bank.why: Spread like wildfire: very fast.

bank.q: The handmade mittens are selling like ___ cakes this winter.
bank.why: Sell like hot cakes: sell fast.

bank.q: The renovation went like ___, on time and under budget.
bank.why: Go like clockwork: as planned. No article.

bank.q: Our grandson took to skating like a ___ to water.
bank.why: Like a duck to water: naturally and easily.

bank.q: The leaked memo spread like a wildfire through the ministry.
bank.why: Usually no article: spread like wildfire.

bank.q: This old trick for opening jars works as a charm.
bank.why: After a verb, like + noun. As a charm would mean in the role of a charm.

bank.q: My new hiking boots fit like a glove straight out of the box.
bank.why: Correct! Fit like a glove = fit perfectly.

bank.q: The ceremony went like clockwork despite the rain.
bank.why: Correct! Go like clockwork = happen exactly as planned.

bank.a: The rumour spread like wildfire through the small town.
bank.why: Spread like wildfire + where it spread.

bank.a: My teenage son eats like a horse these days.
bank.why: Present simple for a habit; time phrase at the end.

bank.a: The new curtains fit the window like a glove.
bank.why: Fit + object + like a glove.
